body_markdown:
Playing with cars covers a wide variety of activities. From toys to multi-million dollar driving tours, it’s possible to engage with the automotive hobby at whatever level you like. For a lot of us, the hobby eventually ends up with a project car. That’s not a good or bad thing, but it is a fact. Don’t believe me? You might have a project car and not even realize it. Here are six indicators that individually might not make a clear decision, but if you check a couple of these boxes… What is your project this weekend?


## Money disappears and packages materialize


Check 404: Money not found.


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


It’s no secret that cars are an expensive hobby, but the steady trickle of spending just to keep a car roadworthy and enjoyable can be sneakily expensive. It’s often hidden by the excitement of the parts, tools, or other solutions appearing on the doormat. If the excitement in the garage is strong enough, it’s easy for eyes to glaze over, and suddenly a car build that was unsponsored is now unofficially sponsored by the credit supplier who gave you enough limit to buy the cam kit and full exhaust. Don’t worry, that rumble will still sound good when the payments start.


## There is no storage space


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


In years of traveling and networking with other car lovers, the one thing I’ve never heard is, “It’s great, I have all the space I need here.”


While constructed of steel, rubber, and plastic, cars are actually a liquid because they expand to fill the container they are put into.[Garages fill with the spare parts](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/6-storage-tips-to-optimize-your-garage-space/) that we know will be hard to find when we need them, upgrades that we haven’t gotten around to doing yet, a second project for all the spare time we have, tools, and of course the fun trinkets and novelties that just come with being engaged in the car world. Your daily driver likely didn’t add anything to the garage, but project cars always do.


## Extra bolts


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Where did they come from? Honestly, it’s better if we don’t remember. Call it being able to do more with less or re-engineer the thing better than the original design team, but sometimes bolts and other hardware just materialize. In a perfect world, it would never happen because we would be too organized to ever misplace hardware, but we live in the real world. Be it[a bolt](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/heres-everything-the-head-of-a-bolt-can-tell-you/) that genuinely is not needed or a brace or questionable utility, there is always a drawer or pile of these bolts hanging around the shop. If you’ve got one, you likely own or have owned project cars.


## Tools living in the trunk


[Kyle Smith](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/kyle-smith/)


Can you trust your car on every trip, every time? I know I can’t, and while that instills a certain amount of excitement in life, it does prove to me that not only is my car not complete, but *it* sometimes is the one that decides when it needs work done. Do you carry a spare part or two to address—just in case—the things you know are questionable but aren’t ready to deal with yet? Yeah, that sounds like a project that has reached or maintained a functional state, but we all know how quickly a completed project devolves right back into just a project. Hint: It’s crazy fast.


## Having “nice jeans”


Getty Images


You know the pair. The ones that garner a side-eye from your significant other when you are doing anything other than going out to dinner or maybe the office. Of course, the first time you forget you’ve got your good pants on and pick up a small project, only to end up with a glob of grease, you have proven that you don’t own a car; you own a project car. And now another pair of “shop pants.”
